Reframed interpretation incorporating SLOOS evidence:
- Policy stance: The FOMC raised the target range to 4.75%–5% and maintained a bias toward “some additional firming,” citing elevated inflation, uncertainty, and policy lags. Balance sheet runoff continues. Implementation settings include IORB at 4.9%, ON RRP at 4.8%, and a primary credit rate of 5%.
- SLOOS read-through on credit supply and demand: Banks are tightening standards on C&I and CRE loans, and reporting weaker loan demand across CRE segments (nonfarm nonresidential, construction and land development, multifamily). Banks also cite decreased investment in plant and equipment and reduced financing needs for mergers and acquisitions, inventories, and accounts receivable. Foreign banks report weaker C&I demand as well. This points to broad-based tightening via the bank-lending channel beyond the policy rate.
- Macro implications: The SLOOS corroborates the Committee’s expectation that recent developments will tighten credit conditions and weigh on activity and hiring. It implies a stronger drag on capex and payrolls and heightens downside risks to growth, while reinforcing a disinflationary impulse from weaker demand. This could reduce the need for aggressive additional hikes even as the Committee remains attentive to inflation risks.
- Net tone: Policy remains cautiously hawkish on inflation, but SLOOS-driven tightening and weaker demand deepen the negative growth/credit outlook relative to the statement alone.
